about: I'm dropped into a sealed barrow with a lantern and an Elvish sword, and from there into the caverns of the Wizard of Frobozz. It's a reworking of Zork II. You pick your way across ravines and through a formal garden with a unicorn, ride a carousel room that spins and sends you off at random, run the bases in a glassy baseball-diamond maze, trick a key out from under a locked door, and try to get treasure out of a ruined Bank of Zork whose doorways know when you're carrying its property. All the while a doddering wizard keeps popping in to cast spells on you that all start with F.

done.why: The world told me I'd used all 300 turns. I was partway through the bank, heading back for Flathead's portrait, and I still hadn't dealt with the dragon or Cerberus, or worked out the menhir. A lot of those turns went on my own fumbling: I fired off long runs of repeated 'examine bag', 'examine brick' and 'look' commands by accident, and at one point all those repeats left me sitting frozen through a Wizard spell.

moments.note: The Wizard turns up out of nowhere, shouts 'Fear!', and I scramble off down the tunnel without meaning to. Great first meeting.
Trying to go back north: 'You may not recall, but when you entered, the door of the barrow shut behind you.' Nice dry nod to the previous game.
Petting the unicorn. It 'melts into the hedges', unsurprised that I'm 'the uncouth sort of vagabond it suspected you were.'
Under the Fantasize spell the garden shows me 'a convention of wizards', and when it wears off the room 'settles down and is only a room.'
The carousel room throws me somewhere random. It does explain why at least, and hints there's machinery somewhere that could stop it.
In the diamond maze I lost the count and couldn't tell how to start over. Wrong steps just dumped me back with the window dark.
Examining the window tells me exactly how the scoreboard counts: flicker, dim, glow, brightest for home. Once I knew that, the puzzle was fair.
Ran all the bases and heard 'a strange rusty squeal'. The floor at the foot of the stairs swung open onto a secret passage.
Ferment made me too unsteady to take the secret passage. It took several tries.
Cerberus scratches its bare necks 'the way a dog does that has lost something it was used to wearing'. A clear hint that it needs a collar.
Place mat under the door, letter opener in the keyhole, pull the mat back, and the rusty key comes out with it. Classic, and very satisfying to pull off.
In the sphere I saw a sandy floor under water, dressed stone, and a shadow passing overhead. Somewhere I haven't been yet.
The dragon catches sight of itself in my brass lamp and 'does not care for the look of the other dragon in it at all.' I wanted to use that.
Frozen solid by the Wizard while my accidental 'look' spam piled up.
I couldn't figure out the bank curtain. It kept sending me to the Small Room, the Vault, or one of the viewing rooms, and I didn't see the pattern.

Worked it out: the curtain takes you somewhere depending on which way you came into the Depository. Coming in from the Chairman's office lands you in the Small Room, and coming in from one teller's room lands you in the opposite viewing room.

Dropped the treasures in the Depository, stepped out to a teller's room and back, picked them up, went through the curtain into a viewing room, then walked south out of the bank. Got the 200 zorkmid bills out.

wished: I wished I'd had the turns to bring the brass lamp to the dragon and see what the reflection hint leads to.
I wanted to find the collar for Cerberus and go through the archway past him.
I wanted to stop the carousel. The game tells me 'a thing that is turned can presumably be stopped, by somebody who finds the works', and I never found them.
I wanted to move the menhir with the 'F' carved on it.
I wished there were a quicker way to restart the count in the diamond maze once it was lost.
I wished the Small Room's other walls did something. Hitting my head on the east wall told me nothing.

lines.line: You may not recall, but when you entered, the door of the barrow shut behind you. There is no way out.
lines.why: It traps you in the world right away, with a wink.

lines.line: The unicorn, unsurprised by this evidence that you are indeed the uncouth sort of vagabond it suspected you were, melts into the hedges and is gone.
lines.why: Funny, and it made me sorry I'd done it.

lines.line: It will wait for her. You need not.
lines.why: From the unicorn's description. A gentle way of telling me the key isn't for me yet.

lines.line: a flicker for first, a dim glow for second, a glow for third, and brightest of all for home, which is where whatever is being counted began; and it goes dark when the count is lost
lines.why: This line is what made the maze solvable.

lines.line: Its necks are bare, and it keeps scratching at them with a hind foot the size of a cart, the way a dog does that has lost something it was used to wearing.
lines.why: A hint that reads like an observation.

lines.line: he has caught sight of himself in the polished brass of your lamp, and that he does not care for the look of the other dragon in it at all.
lines.why: The best hint in the game. I really wanted to follow it up.

lines.line: as though the dragons had come by afterwards and had views.
lines.why: Dry humour about the burnt frescoes.

lines.line: It is not the kind of thing one goes north through; it is the kind of thing one goes through.
lines.why: It taught me the right verb for the curtain without just telling me.

lines.line: It is the doorway that bars it, not the room: the Bank built its doorways to know its own property going through them, and whatever you are carrying, they know. The curtain of light was not built by the same people.
lines.why: It laid out the rules of the bank puzzle as a story.

fun.why: The puzzles were satisfying when they clicked: the baseball diamond, the key under the door, and getting the bills out of the bank. The Wizard's random spells were funny, though sometimes they got in the way. A lot of my frustration came from my own runs of repeated commands, not from the world.

engagement.why: There was always a new room or a fresh hint pulling me on, like the vision in the sphere, Cerberus's bare necks, and the dragon's reflection. I ran out of turns while I still wanted to keep going.

difficulty.why: The bank and the diamond maze were hard, but the world gave clues that made them fair: the window's scoreboard, and the doorways that 'know' what you carry. Running out of lamp battery and turns makes the fumbling cost something.

interestingness.why: It's a familiar old map, but there are new touches that build puzzles in. The window spells out the counting rule, the carousel says it can be stopped, and the doorways explain the bank. They make it feel reasoned rather than arbitrary.

prose.why: The descriptions are wry, specific, and full of character. The unicorn's disdain, the dragons that 'had views', and the portrait's 'great deal of chin' all stuck with me.
